---
title: "Policy Gradient"
description: "A reinforcement-learning method that directly adjusts a policy to increase expected reward."
term: "Policy Gradient"
letter: "P"
category: "Reinforcement Learning"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

A policy gradient method improves an agent's decision rule by nudging it
toward actions that tend to earn more reward. Instead of first learning only
which action is best, it directly learns how the policy should choose.

## Technical explanation

For a parameterized policy $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, policy-gradient methods
estimate the gradient of expected return with respect to parameters
$\theta$. A common form uses sampled returns and
$\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)$, optionally multiplied by an
advantage estimate and adjusted with a baseline to reduce variance.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Direct policy optimization works with stochastic policies and continuous
actions, and underlies widely used reinforcement-learning algorithms.
However, gradient estimates can be noisy, and training behavior depends on
reward design, sampling, and implementation details.

## How it works

The agent collects trajectories under its current policy, calculates
returns or advantages, and updates policy parameters to increase the
probability of actions associated with higher-than-expected return.
Algorithms such as REINFORCE and PPO use different estimators and update
constraints.

## Practical example

In a simulated robot task, the policy maps sensor observations to a
distribution over motor commands. After each rollout, the learner uses
reward and advantage estimates to adjust the policy, then tests the updated
policy on separate seeds and scenarios.

## Common misconceptions

- A policy gradient is an optimization direction estimate, not a guarantee
  that every update improves real-world performance.
- Reward maximization only reflects the reward specification; it does not
  automatically encode safety or intended behavior.
